title: GCD Boundary Formula for Lattice Points on a Segment
description: Proves the GCD boundary formula: the segment from (0,0) to (a,b) contains exactly gcd(a,b)+1 integer lattice points, parameterized by k ↦ (k·(a/g), k·(b/g)) for k=0,...,g. Complete proof: injectivity of the parameterization (at least one of a/g or b/g is positive), and completeness via coprimality (gcd(a/g, b/g)=1 forces p|x from x·q=y·p). 13 theorems, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: card_segmentPoints: the GCD boundary formula — gcd(a,b)+1 lattice points on segment (0,0)→(a,b)
onSegment_mem_segmentPoints: completeness — every segment lattice point is parameterized by some k
segmentPoint_on_segment: soundness — every parameterized point lies on the segment
segmentMap_injective: injectivity — the map k ↦ (k·(a/g), k·(b/g)) is injective when gcd>0
onSegment_iff_mem: complete membership characterization combining soundness and completeness
segment_coprime: when gcd(a,b)=1, the only lattice points are the two endpoints
segment_diagonal: the diagonal (0,0)→(a,a) has a+1 lattice points
pick_edge_contribution: each edge contributes gcd(|Δx|,|Δy|) to Pick's boundary count B

overview.historicalContext: The GCD boundary formula is a classical result in lattice geometry, underlying Pick's theorem (1899): for a lattice polygon with area A, interior lattice points I, and boundary lattice points B, we have A = I + B/2 - 1. The boundary count B = Σ gcd(|Δxᵢ|, |Δyᵢ|) summed over edges, since each edge from (x₁,y₁) to (x₂,y₂) contributes gcd(|x₂-x₁|, |y₂-y₁|) points when shared endpoints are accounted for. The formula connects elementary number theory (coprimality, Euclidean algorithm) with two-dimensional geometry.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize the GCD boundary formula: the number of integer lattice points on the segment from (0,0) to (a,b) is gcd(a,b)+1. Prove completeness (every lattice point is parameterized) using coprimality of a/g and b/g.
overview.text: The segment from (0,0) to (a,b) contains exactly gcd(a,b)+1 lattice points: the points (k·(a/g), k·(b/g)) for k=0,1,...,g where g=gcd(a,b). These are all lattice points on the segment and there are no others.
overview.proofStrategy: Define segmentPoints as the image of {0,...,g} under k ↦ (k·(a/g), k·(b/g)). Prove injectivity: at least one of a/g or b/g is positive when g>0, so the map is injective on first or second component. Prove completeness via coprimality: from x·b = y·a with a=g·p, b=g·q and gcd(p,q)=1, we derive x·q = y·p (dividing by g), then p | x·q with p⊥q gives p | x, so x = k·p and y = k·q for some k ≤ g.
keyInsights: The parameterization k ↦ (k·(a/g), k·(b/g)) is injective because when g = gcd(a,b) > 0, at least one of a/g or b/g is positive: if a/g = 0 then a=0 so g=b and b/g = b/b = 1 > 0
Coprimality of a/g and b/g (via Nat.coprime_div_gcd_div_gcd) is the key to completeness: from x·q = y·p with gcd(p,q)=1, deduce p | x, giving the unique k
The formula gcd(a,b)+1 is consistent at the boundary cases: gcd(0,0)=0 gives 1 point {(0,0)}; gcd(a,a)=a gives a+1 diagonal points; gcd(p,q)=1 coprime gives 2 endpoints
The proof works over ℕ directly without needing ℤ, handling the a=0 and b=0 cases separately from the generic coprimality argument
The edge contribution to Pick's theorem is gcd(|Δx|,|Δy|) (= card-1): this is the number of shared-endpoint-excluded lattice points on each edge
prerequisites: GCD and coprimality: Nat.gcd, Nat.Coprime, Nat.coprime_div_gcd_div_gcd

sections.title: Definitions
sections.summary: Defines onSegment (collinearity + bounds) and segmentPoints (image of {0,...,g} under the parameterization k ↦ (k·(a/g), k·(b/g))).

sections.title: Soundness: Parameterized Points Are on Segment
sections.summary: segmentPoint_on_segment: (k·(a/g), k·(b/g)) satisfies collinearity (via calc with ring) and bounds (k ≤ g gives k·(a/g) ≤ g·(a/g) = a). mem_segmentPoints_on_segment follows.

sections.title: Injectivity of the Parameterization
sections.summary: segmentMap_injective: case split on a/g=0 vs a/g>0. When a=0, g=b and b/g=1, use second component. When a/g>0, use first component with Nat.eq_of_mul_eq_mul_right.
sections.mathContext: Either $a/g > 0$ (use $k_1 \cdot (a/g) = k_2 \cdot (a/g) \Rightarrow k_1 = k_2$) or $a=0$ so $g=b$ and $b/g=1$ (use $k_1 = k_2$).

sections.title: GCD Boundary Formula
sections.summary: card_segmentPoints: when gcd=0 (a=b=0), exactly 1 point. When gcd>0, injectivity gives card = card(range(g+1)) = g+1.

sections.title: Completeness: All Segment Points Parameterized
sections.summary: onSegment_mem_segmentPoints: three cases. gcd=0: trivial. a=0: k=y works directly. a>0: coprimality argument using Nat.coprime_div_gcd_div_gcd and Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right.
sections.mathContext: From $x \cdot q = y \cdot p$ and $\gcd(p,q)=1$: $p \mid x \cdot q$ so $p \mid x$, giving $x = kp$, $y = kq$, $k \leq g$.

sections.title: Special Cases and Pick's Formula
sections.summary: segment_coprime (2 endpoints), segment_diagonal (a+1 points), three concrete examples, pick_edge_contribution and interior_segment_count for Pick's theorem boundary formula.
sections.mathContext: $B = \sum_i \gcd(|\Delta x_i|, |\Delta y_i|)$, with each edge contributing $\text{card} - 1 = \gcd(a,b)$.

conclusion.summary: Fully proves the GCD boundary formula for lattice points on a segment: card(segmentPoints(a,b)) = gcd(a,b)+1. The proof is machine-verified with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. Key techniques: Finset.card_image_of_injective for the cardinality, Nat.coprime_div_gcd_div_gcd + Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right for completeness. 13 theorems, 2 definitions, 245 lines.
conclusion.implications: This formula is the foundation of the boundary count B in Pick's theorem. A polygon with n edges, each going from (xᵢ,yᵢ) to (xᵢ₊₁,yᵢ₊₁), has boundary count B = Σ gcd(|Δxᵢ|, |Δyᵢ|). With this formula formalized, a constructive proof of Pick's theorem (as opposed to the axiomatized version) requires formalizing triangulation of lattice polygons.
openQuestions: Can Pick's theorem itself be fully proved in Lean by combining this GCD formula with a triangulation argument (ear-clipping or diagonal decomposition)?
Generalize to lattice points in a tetrahedron: the number of integer points on the segment from (0,0,0) to (a,b,c) is gcd(a,b,c)+1
Ehrhart polynomial generalization: for a lattice polytope P, the count of lattice points in tP is a polynomial in t (Pick is the t=1, d=2 case)

crossReferences.description: Pick's Theorem via Triangulation — the OQ about whether the GCD formula can give a constructive proof of Pick's theorem.
Pick's Theorem — the original formalization whose boundary count B uses the GCD formula proved here.
